title: Pears in Red Wine
subtitle: Whole pears poached slowly in spiced red wine until deep crimson
excerpt: Firm pears peeled and poached whole in spiced red wine until they take on a deep, glossy crimson colour and the wine reduces to a syrup. A classic French-British dessert that improves considerably if made a day ahead.
sourceNotes: Pears poached in red wine are a fixture of both French bourgeois cooking and British dinner-party menus from the 1970s onwards. Jane Grigson and Elizabeth David both give versions. The key is a firm pear, Williams or Conference, that holds its shape through the long poaching time.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make 1 day ahead and refrigerate in the syrup. The pears deepen in colour and the flavour concentrates further overnight. Serve cold or gently warmed.

content.text: Pears in red wine is a deceptively simple dessert, whole peeled pears standing upright in a pan of spiced red wine, simmered for 40 to 45 minutes until the flesh softens and turns crimson all the way through, and the wine reduces to a syrup that coats them glossily. Use a firm pear: Conference or Williams hold their shape; Comice will collapse. The result is better made the day before and served cold.

items.prepNote: firm variety (Conference or Williams), peeled, stalks left on

content.text: Combine the red wine, orange juice, sugar, cinnamon stick, cloves, allspice, and vanilla pod in a saucepan wide enough to hold the pears standing upright. Heat over a medium heat, stirring until the sugar has dissolved. Taste and adjust, it should be pleasantly sweet and spiced, not overpoweringly so.

Peel the pears, leaving the stalks intact for presentation. Use a melon baller or teaspoon to remove the core from the base of each pear. Stand the pears upright in the simmering liquid, they should be nearly submerged. If they are not, add a splash more wine or water.

Cover with a circle of baking paper pressed directly on the surface of the liquid (a cartouche), then put the lid on. Simmer over a low heat for 35 to 45 minutes, turning the pears occasionally, until a skewer slides into the thickest part of the pear with no resistance. The pears should be a deep, even crimson throughout.

Remove the pears carefully and set aside. Boil the remaining liquid over a high heat for 8 to 12 minutes until it has reduced to a glossy, syrupy consistency that coats the back of a spoon lightly. Strain out the spices. Pour the syrup over the pears and leave to cool. Serve cold or at room temperature with the syrup spooned over, and crème fraîche or whipped cream alongside.

items.symptom: The pears are not taking on colour
items.cause: The pears are only partially submerged, or the heat is too low.
items.fix: Turn the pears regularly during poaching, and ensure the liquid is at a steady simmer. A weighted piece of baking paper (cartouche) pressed onto the surface helps.

items.symptom: The pears are overcooked and collapsing
items.cause: A soft variety was used, or the poaching time was too long.
items.fix: Use Conference or Williams pears and check with a skewer at 35 minutes. Remove them from the liquid the moment they are tender.
Continue reducing until it coats a spoon. It also thickens considerably as it cools, remove from heat a little before it seems done.

content.text: Keeps in the fridge in the syrup for up to 3 days. The colour and flavour deepen in storage, making this one of the few desserts that is better on day two.
